minutes.headline: Finance Committee recommended against the school override and put off the school's free-cash fallback plan
minutes.summary: The Finance Committee held its warrant-article public hearing and voted its recommendation on nearly every FY26 town meeting article, including the omnibus budget, two debt-exclusion projects (Marshall Park and the municipal building/Ritter renovation), and a slate of enterprise-fund and stabilization transfers. It recommended disapproval of the citizens'-petition Proposition 2½ override and deferred a recommendation on the conditional $500,000 free-cash transfer to schools pending details of how the money would be spent, then spent the balance of the meeting workshopping its own annual town-meeting report, including a member's independent review of the school department's staffing-cut and budget-growth figures.

public_comment.topic: Objected to the DPW's cemetery-road capital request without a topography/wetlands plan; proposed an electrical-infrastructure alternative instead.

public_comment.stated_role: Presidential Highway, Jefferson NH, formerly of Lunenburg
public_comment.topic: General remarks before addressing the reserve fund transfer article.
Cautioned that the reserve fund is for true emergencies only, not for departments that overspend a line item.
Continued objection to the cemetery road capital item, alleging no wetlands filing and a possible patronage motive; asked the committee to redirect the funds to electrical work instead.
Defended the DPW director's cemetery capital request as normal, vetted capital-planning process; said full expansion is years away.
Asked what the financial impact is of the SAP grade-adjustment articles.
A resident (using John Bowen's earlier self-introduction) argued the DPW director is grossly underpaid and that pay adjustments should start from the top of the org chart down.
Asked whether the new communications/IT position would be budgeted for family-plan health insurance, as the prior town manager's practice was.
Asked about the PEG/PAC access program's reported budget deficit and how it will be sustained.
Asked about the town manager's discretion over hardship property-tax exemptions.
Explained his citizens-petition article (32) requiring a warrant-article vote before cemetery commission funds can be spent, citing past unplanned spending.
Asked whether the town's debt-capacity projections accounted for a future Turkey Hill Elementary borrowing need.
Asked for the tax impact on the average homeowner from the Marshall Park debt exclusion.
Warned that the municipal building/Ritter project's cost estimate could grow further before construction, as has happened before.
Raised concern about state-mandated heat pumps driving up new building operating costs, citing recent elevator and HVAC costs.
A resident with HVAC/cost-estimating experience recommended using RS Means software to properly estimate the new building's future operating costs and suggested budgeting a large contingency.
Thanked the member who cast the dissenting vote on the municipal building article and urged the committee to remember employee compensation fairness when the building is built.
Thanked the Finance Committee for its work through a difficult budget season.

budget_items.topic: Fire dept vehicle maintenance reserve fund transfer
budget_items.what_was_said: The fire chief requested a reserve fund transfer to cover an ambulance diesel particulate filter/exhaust repair after vehicle maintenance funds ran low. He noted the line typically covers fuel and one significant repair a year.

budget_items.topic: Article 2 - borrowing in anticipation of revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: A new fail-safe article to allow the town to borrow if there is a cash-flow shortfall from revenues not coming in as expected; select board recommended it at 50.
A variety of capital projects were bundled into one article, including a disputed $50,000 cemetery road item that a resident wanted redirected to electrical infrastructure instead.

budget_items.topic: Special projects funding / grant writing pilot (Article 9)
budget_items.what_was_said: Following prior discussion, crack-seal/cemetery road repairs were swapped out for a grant writing services pilot proposal in this article.
The town manager presented the omnibus budget total, unchanged from the prior presentation; the committee noted ongoing conversations with departments before town meeting.
A citizen's petition sought a Proposition 2½ override; select board voted not to recommend it and not to place it on the ballot, though it may still appear via the citizens' petition process.

budget_items.topic: $500,000 free cash transfer to schools, conditioned on override failing (Article 12)
budget_items.what_was_said: This transfer would only occur if the override fails; the committee deferred its recommendation pending a school presentation on how the money would be spent.

budget_items.topic: SAP grade adjustments - DPW director and communications/IT manager (Article 13)
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said upgrading the DPW director's grade and expanding a part-time communications/IT position to full-time would each cost roughly $10,000, funded from the salary reserve line.

budget_items.topic: Insurance cost for new full-time position
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident noted that historically a $10,000 salary increase for a new full-time hire could carry roughly a $35,000 total budget impact once family health insurance is included.
The town manager's proposed non-union pay plan increase moved from 2.5% to 3%, an estimated $43,000 total impact, while the clerical union received a larger negotiated increase.
Paying call firefighters time-and-a-half for holiday shifts was estimated at up to $6,000 based on holidays falling on Sundays.
These free-cash-to-stabilization transfers are the ones being effectively redirected to fund the $500,000 school transfer; the committee recommended no action, following the select board.
A free cash transfer to the town's other-post-employment-benefits trust fund, which is only about 2.69% funded, was recommended as this should not be skipped.
A new reserve fund to cover unbudgeted accrued vacation/sick time payouts when employees separate, funded with $10,000 from free cash.
A bundle of sewer-enterprise transfers covering OPEB liability, the FY26 sewer operating budget, inflow/infiltration stabilization, and reserve capacity stabilization.
Pay-as-you-throw bag revenues fund the trash portion of the solid waste program; a bag price increase was flagged as a likely future discussion.
A transfer from water enterprise revenues to operate the water enterprise fund for FY26.
The public access program is drawing down its reserves this year by roughly $30,000 and is expected to need closer attention as cable-based revenue continues to decline.

A debt exclusion requiring both town meeting and ballot approval; estimated tax rate impact ranged by amortization term, with the chair's own debt-capacity analysis showing the town stays within its 11% excludable debt policy in most years.

budget_items.topic: Municipal building / Ritter Memorial renovation debt exclusion (Article 34)
budget_items.what_was_said: A debt exclusion to renovate town hall into a meeting house and expand Ritter building for municipal and school offices; residents raised concerns about unknown future operating costs and contingency adequacy.

budget_items.topic: Net state aid figure for the annual report
budget_items.what_was_said: The committee tried to insert the net state aid figure into the draft annual report; the number was repeated several times with inconsistent digits in the captions.

budget_items.topic: State aid growth rate history for annual report
budget_items.what_was_said: The draft report noted state aid grew roughly 5.3% annually from FY13 to FY24 but slowed to about 1.5% over the last three years.

The draft annual report initially cited exact school staffing cut figures; the committee changed the language to 'approximately' because the school committee had not finalized which positions would be cut.

budget_items.topic: Tax rate impact of the school override (annual report)
budget_items.what_was_said: The draft report calculated that, if approved, the override would add about 89 cents per thousand to the tax rate, equating to roughly a stated dollar amount and percentage increase for the average single-family home.
The report describes Lunenburg as one of six of 197 Massachusetts fire departments still running three shifts rather than four, with 62% of coverage from call/per-diem staff.

budget_items.topic: Chair's independent analysis of the school budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair walked through his own calculation comparing the school department's FY25 and FY26 budget, staffing-cut percentages, and revenue figures, arguing they imply a much larger increase than presented and that the school's staffing counts do not reconcile across their own documents.

decisions.decision: Town meeting date confirmed as May 3, 2025.
Committee agreed to vote on each warrant article as they went through them, rather than voting on all at the end.
Noted that article numbers may still change before town meeting.
Chair agreed to follow up directly with the municipal building design committee chair on projected operating costs for the new building.
Committee agreed to add percentage figures alongside per-thousand tax rate figures in the annual report for both debt exclusion projects.
Chair given authorization to make final editorial edits to the annual report after the meeting.
Members agreed to read outstanding draft minutes before the next meeting so they can be approved.
Committee agreed to look into alternative methods of recording minutes, such as Zoom transcription software.
Next meeting set for April 10th (or possibly the 17th/24th, chair to confirm by email), given no pressing agenda items expected before then.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee voted to recommend disapproval of the citizens'-petition override headed to town meeting.
It deferred any recommendation on a conditional free-cash transfer to schools, pending a school spending plan.
It recommended approval of the FY26 omnibus budget and the full FY26 capital program.
It recommended approval of two debt exclusions, splitting 5-1 on the municipal building/Ritter renovation.
The committee approved its own annual town meeting report, with the chair authorized to make edits.

why_it_matters: Town meeting voters will decide the override themselves; the committee's recommendation is advice, not a veto.
The schools' free-cash transfer only happens if the override fails, so the two votes are linked outcomes for school funding.
Both debt exclusions would add to property tax bills if approved at town meeting, separate from the annual budget.
